characters: Maaya: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, with a notebook and pencil.
Paa: her classmate, 13, in a white shirt and navy shorts, always asking questions.
Madam Ankrah: their history teacher, in a green dress, carrying a folder of maps.
Elmina Castle: a large white fort beside the blue sea, with palm trees and fishing boats nearby.

narrationPlan.voice: Calm, clear storyteller voice; Madam Ankrah is warm and exact
narrationPlan.pace: Steady and clear, slower on the hard part of the story (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle waves and a slow, low drum; a quiet, respectful tune for the hard part (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Elmina Castle is a World Heritage Site and a national museum. This story uses published accounts and invented pupils and teachers.
The story is plain about the trade in enslaved people and avoids graphic detail. Teachers should be ready to answer questions calmly and truthfully.
The story shows that people on this coast were already trading gold before the Portuguese came, so that Ghanaians are not shown only as people things happened to.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: Portuguese arrival in 1471; fleet arrived 19 January 1482 and building began the next day; Diogo de Azambuja; King John II; the Dutch attempt in 1596; capture in 1637; Dutch trade in enslaved people until 1814; UNESCO inscription in 1979.
The meaning “Saint George of the Mine” and the origin of the name “Elmina” should be confirmed against a published source before release.
The Columbus claim is contested and is shown as such; check the wording with a historian.
Ask the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board or a local guide to review the story.

teacherGuide.overview: A history story about one building and three centuries of change. It teaches that a place can have more than one purpose, that evidence has gaps, and that remembering hard history is a form of respect.
learningGoals: Explain why Elmina Castle was built and how its use changed.
Place events on a timeline and calculate time between them.
Explain how historians handle conflicting dates.

subjectLinks.link: Europeans on the Gold Coast and the trade in enslaved people

beforeReading: Ask: what building in your town has more than one history? Who might know it?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to list the three uncertain dates and say how they would find out more.
afterReading: Draw a timeline from 1471 to 2026 with the dates in the story.
Write three questions you would ask a museum guide.
discussion: Why does it matter that gold trade existed here before the fort?
Why keep a building linked to painful history?
reflection: What is one thing from our past that we should never forget?

mathsExtension.task: From 1482 to 2026 is how many years?
From the Dutch capture in 1637 to the end of their trade in enslaved people in 1814 is how many years?
The Portuguese reached the coast in 1471 and began building in 1482. How many years passed?

support: Give learners a blank timeline with the five dates to place.
stretch: Find out how gold reached the coast from inland and who carried it.

whatWeKnow: The castle was begun by the Portuguese in January 1482 and was later held by the Dutch.
It was used in the trade in enslaved people.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a museum.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The exact dates of some transfers of power, which sources give differently.
Whether Christopher Columbus sailed on a 1481 voyage.

factCheck.claim: The Portuguese built the castle; the fleet arrived on 19 January 1482 and building began the next morning; Diogo de Azambuja led the fleet; King John II ordered the fort; the Dutch tried in 1596 and captured it in 1637; the Dutch continued the trade in enslaved people until 1814; UNESCO inscribed the site in 1979.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s Elmina Castle article, which also notes that some sources give 1642 for the Dutch takeover of the Portuguese Gold Coast and that the Columbus claim is not settled.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Elmina Castle”. Check also scholarly histories of Elmina and the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
